title: Show the same questions in a different order
goal: Every participant sees all the questions; only the order changes.
steps: Keep the questions that must always come first (such as consent and eligibility) outside the shuffled set.
Open your survey, select Structure, and edit the first question you want to shuffle.
In its advanced question settings, find Randomization group name. Enter a short shared name such as SHUFFLE1.
Enter exactly SHUFFLE1 for every other question that should switch places. Leave this setting empty on questions that must remain fixed.
Save each question, then use Preview survey to test a fresh session.
check: All intended questions still appear.
Their order changes across independent starts; a single participant’s order remains stable.
Question codes and recorded answers remain aligned.
mistakes: A randomization group changes order; it does not hide questions.
Preview survey, not just Preview question group, for reliable checking.
note: Guidance based on LimeSurvey documentation; exact placement and behavior have not been verified on the Kassel 3.28 installation.

title: Show complete question groups in a random order
goal: The three research sections appear in different orders, but each section stays together.
steps: Create a separate question group for each complete block (for example Brand Trust, Satisfaction, Purchase Intention).
Open Structure, edit the first question group, and find Randomization group.
Enter a common label such as BLOCKORDER. Save.
Enter the same label for the other groups that should change order.
Keep consent, screening and final debrief groups outside this randomization set.
Preview the full survey several times using fresh starts.
check: The chosen groups switch order between fresh sessions.
Questions stay within their assigned group.
All blocks still appear.
mistakes: Shuffling groups is not assigning participants to a single experimental condition.
Do not shuffle a group that is logically dependent on responses to a later group.
note: Guidance based on LimeSurvey documentation; exact placement and behavior have not been verified on the Kassel 3.28 installation.

title: Shuffle answer choices in a single-choice list
goal: A list of product brands appears in different orders to reduce position effects.
steps: Open a single-choice List (radio) question with several independent answer options.
Open advanced question settings and find Random answer order.
Choose Yes and save the question.
Preview the whole survey in separate fresh sessions and observe whether choices move.
If your question includes Other, None of the above or Don’t know, verify its behavior separately before launching.
check: Response labels move across fresh sessions.
Answer codes remain attached to their intended labels.
Special options behave as intended.
mistakes: Do not shuffle ordered categories such as Strongly Disagree to Strongly Agree.
For matrix questions with subquestions, this setting may shuffle statements rather than response columns.
note: Guidance based on LimeSurvey documentation; exact placement and behavior have not been verified on the Kassel 3.28 installation.

title: Shuffle the statements in a Likert matrix
goal: Participants rate the same statements but see them in a different row order.
steps: Open the relevant Array question.
Check that each statement has its own stable subquestion code.
Under advanced settings select Random answer order = Yes (in this case it applies to subquestions).
Save and preview the complete survey from several fresh starts.
Export a test dataset later and verify that data fields still match the intended statement codes.
check: Matrix rows change order, but column labels remain in logical order.
Each statement retains its underlying code.
mistakes: Do not assume Random answer order shuffles the columns of an array.
Keep multi-part questions together if their order conveys meaning.
note: Guidance based on LimeSurvey documentation; exact placement and behavior have not been verified on the Kassel 3.28 installation.

title: Understand random order, random selection and random assignment
goal: Choose the correct method before you change any setting.
steps: Random ORDER means everyone sees Q1, Q2 and Q3, but in different orders.
Random SELECTION means some questions are hidden, so a person might see only Q2.
Random ASSIGNMENT means a person receives one condition, such as advertisement A or advertisement B.
Decide which of these outcomes your research design requires.
Write the expected outcome on paper before editing LimeSurvey.
check: You can describe your desired outcome in one sentence.
You do not confuse changing order with hiding content.
mistakes: A randomization group name generally changes order only.
Random assignment does not guarantee equal group sizes.
note: Guidance based on LimeSurvey documentation; exact placement and behavior have not been verified on the Kassel 3.28 installation.

title: What is an Equation question and why would I use it?
goal: Store a calculated value that later questions can use.
steps: An Equation question is a calculation field, not a question requiring an answer from the participant.
Create an Equation question with a short code such as COND.
For a simple demonstration enter {2+3} as its equation text and check that it evaluates to 5.
Only after verifying the calculation should you use its code in another question’s relevance setting.
Advanced condition assignment requires a value to be calculated once and retained; see the experimental-condition guides.
check: An Equation question produces the expected calculation.
You understand that the value can be referenced by its question code.
mistakes: Curly braces are used in question/equation text; relevance fields use an expression without braces.
Do not repeatedly recalculate a random value in several separate conditions.
words: { and } tell LimeSurvey to evaluate an expression in question text.
note: Guidance based on LimeSurvey documentation; exact placement and behavior have not been verified on the Kassel 3.28 installation.

title: Read the symbols in a relevance equation
goal: Understand the small pieces of a display rule.
steps: Find a question code, such as AGEGROUP. This identifies the earlier question.
Find ==, which means is equal to.
Find the answer code in quotes, such as "1".
Enter AGEGROUP == "1" in a later question’s relevance equation field if that exact question and answer code exist.
Test once with the matching answer and once with a different answer.
check: The follow-up appears only for the matching answer.
All codes match the actual survey exactly, including uppercase/lowercase.
mistakes: The answer code is not necessarily the number printed beside an answer.
Do not surround a relevance equation with curly braces.
words: AGEGROUP is the earlier question code.
"1" is the stored answer code we want.
note: Guidance based on LimeSurvey documentation; exact placement and behavior have not been verified on the Kassel 3.28 installation.

title: Combine two conditions using AND or OR
goal: Display a question based on more than one earlier answer.
steps: Confirm that both earlier questions have stable codes, for example CONSENT and AGEGROUP.
Choose AND when both conditions must be true; choose OR when either is enough.
Enter CONSENT == "Y" and AGEGROUP == "1" in the later question’s relevance field, assuming those are your real answer codes.
Test all combinations, not just one successful path.
check: With AND, only the combination matching both values shows the question.
With OR, either matching condition shows the question.
mistakes: A capital Y is not the same as a lower-case y in all contexts.
Do not use the text of the answer where the code is required.
words: and requires both checks to be true.
AGEGROUP == "1" checks the selected age category.
note: Guidance based on LimeSurvey documentation; exact placement and behavior have not been verified on the Kassel 3.28 installation.

title: What does a random-number equation mean?
goal: Understand how a condition number can be picked.
steps: Think of three experimental conditions labelled 1, 2 and 3.
The function rand(1,3) is intended to choose one whole number between 1 and 3.
A random value should be calculated once in an early hidden Equation question, then referenced later by its code.
Do not paste rand(1,3) separately into three relevance fields; doing that can give inconsistent results.
Test independent sessions, retained assignments and the response export before collecting real data.
check: You can explain the difference between selecting once and calculating repeatedly.
The stored assignment is available for later checks in a tested survey.
mistakes: Random does not mean equal numbers of participants in each condition.
The exact Equation implementation and hiding behavior still require a LimeSurvey 3.28 test.
words: rand means choose a random whole number.
note: Concept verified in the ExpressionScript reference. The full assignment recipe is not yet locally tested for this installation.

title: Show only one random question from five
goal: Each participant sees just one of five questions rather than all five.
steps: Give each candidate question a distinct code and decide whether they share a page or live in different groups.
Create a hidden assignment Equation before the questions. The official manual contains a “Randomly Ask One Question Per Group” sample survey.
Use the stored assignment code as the reference for five relevance rules, one matching each possible choice.
Test every selected question through multiple fresh starts; check that exactly one is displayed.
Inspect exported test data to verify which question was displayed and whether the assigned value was stored.
check: Exactly one of five candidate questions appears for each fresh session.
All five questions are reachable across test sessions.
mistakes: This is different from shuffling five questions.
Do not copy a sample relevance expression without adapting its codes and survey grouping.
note: Advanced documented approach; not locally verified in the Kassel installation. Use the official sample survey and test configuration before deployment.

title: Show a random subset, such as three questions out of ten
goal: Each participant sees a fixed-size subset chosen from a larger bank.
steps: Put the question bank in a deliberate group, assigning stable codes Q1–Q10.
Consult the official Expression Manager sample “Randomly Ask A Specific Number Of Questions In A Group”.
That method combines random order with relevanceStatus checks; it is not a simple checkbox.
Follow the example in a separate test survey using the same display mode it requires.
Run many fresh previews and verify that exactly three questions appear before using it with participants.
check: Exactly the requested number of items appears.
Question selection changes across new sessions.
The stored responses correspond to the visible questions.
mistakes: The documented example has survey-display-mode restrictions.
Changing an example from five-of-ten to three-of-ten requires careful changes to every relevance rule.
note: Method referenced from official example; step-by-step equations intentionally withheld until locally tested.

title: Show one complete random pair of questions
goal: Each participant sees exactly one predetermined pair, with both questions from that pair.
steps: List your pairs clearly: Pair A has A1 and A2, Pair B has B1 and B2, and so on.
Do not use a common question-randomization name expecting it to choose a pair: that changes order only.
Plan one stored assignment value per participant, calculated before the pairs are shown.
Attach the same condition to both questions of a pair (or to the entire pair group), and a different condition to each other pair.
Test every branch and check that exactly one complete pair is shown, including when participants go back and forward.
check: One pair only appears per participant.
Both members of that pair always appear together.
The assignment remains stable during navigation.
mistakes: Do not evaluate rand() independently on both questions.
Avoid using group-level settings unless you have tested their interaction with the survey display mode.
note: Design pattern explained; not a verified copy-paste implementation for LimeSurvey 3.28.

title: Assign participants to one of three experimental scenarios
goal: Each participant sees one of three scenarios and related questions.
steps: Define the three conditions A, B and C before building the survey.
Create an early assignment field and store a single randomly chosen condition code.
Place each condition’s scenario and follow-up questions in its own clearly named group.
Apply a matching relevance rule to each condition group, referencing the stored code.
Test all three branches, verify stability when navigating backwards, and confirm the condition appears in the exported data.
check: Each participant sees exactly one scenario.
They never see follow-up questions belonging to a different scenario.
The assigned condition can be identified in exported test records.
mistakes: Equal allocation is not guaranteed with simple random assignment.
Do not change condition definitions midway through actual data collection without methodological review.
note: Research design guidance; the exact LimeSurvey 3.28 assignment formula remains untested.

title: Why are all my questions appearing despite randomization?
goal: Diagnose the most common confusion between order and visibility.
steps: Check whether you entered only a Randomization group name; that setting changes order but does not hide questions.
If selective display is intended, inspect each question’s relevance equation.
Confirm the referenced question codes exist and the answer/assignment codes are exact.
Inspect the survey logic/check-logic report, then test from the beginning of a new session.
Confirm that the assignment is evaluated before the affected questions.
check: Only intended content is visible.
The condition does not change unexpectedly on a previous/next page transition.
mistakes: Changing the order and hiding questions are separate operations.
A relevance equation that is always true will not filter the display.
note: Guidance based on LimeSurvey documentation; exact placement and behavior have not been verified on the Kassel 3.28 installation.

title: How to test randomization before launching research
goal: Check both participant experience and recorded results.
steps: Make a copy or use an inactive test survey; never experiment on a live study.
Write down expected behavior for every branch, pair or condition.
Start multiple independent test sessions rather than repeatedly refreshing one response.
Check visual display, back/forward navigation, any special answer options and mobile layouts.
Where possible, activate a separate test copy and export synthetic responses to check the saved condition codes.
Keep a short testing log and correct every discrepancy before collecting real data.
check: Every intended branch has been observed.
No participant sees contradictory scenarios or incomplete pairs.
Exported variables identify assigned conditions when relevant.
mistakes: A successful .lss import does not prove the logic works.
A few trials cannot establish uniform assignment or allocation balance.
note: Guidance based on LimeSurvey documentation; exact placement and behavior have not been verified on the Kassel 3.28 installation.
